rejected.title: Why living standards differ
card: Living standards describe how well off people are, such as whether they can afford food, housing, health care and education. They differ between Australians.
Unemployment and low pay cut the income a household has to spend. A household with little income may struggle to pay for basic needs.
Illness can mean extra costs and less time at work, so income may fall while spending rises. Where people live matters too, as remote areas can have fewer jobs and services.
When income stays too low to meet basic needs for a long time, a household may be in poverty. Some Australians live in poverty.
rejected.remember: Living standards differ because jobs, pay, health and place can change what a household can afford.

a.q: Which of these is a reason two Australian households can have very different living standards?
opts: Unemployment can cut the income one household has to spend
Illness can lower the costs one household has to pay
Low pay can give one household more income to spend
Remote areas can give one household more jobs nearby
a.why: Losing a job cuts income, so that household has less to spend on basic needs. The illness option reverses the effect: illness can add costs, such as medical bills, rather than lower them.
a.clue: Check which way each cause moves income or costs.

b.q: Tom lives in a remote town in the Northern Territory. He lost his job, and there are few other jobs nearby. What is the most likely effect on him?
opts: His income may stay low for a while, as few jobs are nearby
His costs may fall, so his living standard may rise
He may find work quickly, as remote towns have more jobs
His spending may rise, as he has more free time to shop
b.why: Losing his job cuts Tom's income, and with few local jobs it may be hard to replace, so his living standard may fall. The quick-work option is tempting, but remote areas can have fewer jobs, not more.
b.clue: Think about the job loss and the town together.

a.q: Which of these best explains why two Australian households can have very different living standards?
opts: Their work, health and place change what they earn and need
Every household spends its income on the same things
Living standards depend only on how large a home is
Households in all towns have the same jobs and services
a.why: Work, pay, health and where people live change both what a household earns and what it must spend. The other options assume households are alike, but the card shows their circumstances differ.
a.clue: Think about what changes the money a household has and needs.

b.q: Tom lives in a remote town in the Northern Territory. He lost his job, and there are few other jobs nearby. Which is the most direct effect on his living standard?
opts: His income falls, so he may struggle to afford basic needs
His wealth rises, so he can buy more goods and services
His health improves, so he spends less on health care
His costs fall, so he can save more than before
b.why: Losing a job cuts income, and few local jobs make it harder to replace. That can make basic needs hard to afford. A fall in income does not raise wealth or savings.
b.clue: What happens to a household's income when a job is lost?

a.best: Their work, health and place change what they earn and need

b.best: His income falls, so he may struggle to afford basic needs

The clue ('what changes the money a household has and needs') echoes the right option's wording ('what they earn and need'), making it easy to match without understanding.
The distractor 'Living standards depend only on how large a home is' uses the absolute 'only', which makes it easy to rule out on wording alone.

a.q: Why can two Australian households end up with very different living standards?
opts: Unemployment can cut what one household has to spend
Illness can lower the costs one household has to pay
Low pay can give one household more income to spend
Remote areas can give one household more jobs nearby
a.why: Losing a job cuts income, so that household has less to spend on basic needs. The illness option reverses the effect: illness can add costs, such as medical bills, rather than lower them.
a.clue: Check which way each cause moves income or costs.

b.q: Tom lives in a remote town in the Northern Territory and loses his job at the local mine. What is the most likely effect on his living standard?
opts: It may fall and stay low, as jobs can be scarce there
It may fall briefly, as remote towns tend to have more jobs
It may rise, as he has more free time and fewer costs
It may stay the same, as remote towns have more services
b.why: Losing his job cuts Tom's income, and remote areas can have fewer jobs, so new work may be hard to find and his living standard may stay low for a while. Remote areas tend to have fewer jobs and services, not more, so a quick recovery is unlikely.
b.clue: Think about the job loss and the town together.

a.best: Unemployment can cut what one household has to spend

b.best: It may fall and stay low, as jobs can be scarce there
